About us

At Pāmu, we are committed to enriching our land, our people, and the future of food and fibre for Aotearoa New Zealand. As the brand name for Landcorp Farming Limited, a State-Owned Enterprise established in 1886, we are proud to be the largest pastoral farming company in New Zealand, managing nearly 360,000 hectares across more than 100 farms. We aim to farm sustainably and responsibly, ensuring that future generations inherit a thriving agricultural landscape. We manage a broad mix of land types and classes, including some of New Zealand’s most iconic farms such as Wairākei Estate and Molesworth Station. Balancing operational performance with environmental stewardship is at the core of everything we do. Our farming approach is rooted in innovation and sustainability. We are constantly evolving our practices to reduce environmental impact, enhance biodiversity, and create long-term value for the land we are entrusted to manage. Our leadership in organic farming, methane-reducing livestock, and conservation efforts are key examples of how we are shaping the future of agriculture. Kaitiakitanga—guardianship of the environment—is fundamental to our operations. We are dedicated to nurturing the land, protecting ecosystems, and reducing our carbon footprint. We’re committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and have protected over 10,000 hectares of conservation land under QEII covenants. As stewards of these natural assets, we strive to enhance both the land and the wider agricultural sector. Our people are at the heart of Pāmu. With 630 permanent staff, we are committed to creating a safe, supportive, and inclusive workplace. We invest in the growth and well-being of our team through comprehensive safety measures, mental health training, and development opportunities.

    #Meet Diane Karaitiana-Bryant, Facility Manager at the St Kilda Methane Research Facility, Pāmu. 🌱 "Clean data doesn't happen by accident." That's how Diane sums up her approach to running one of the key research sites within Pāmu. As Facility Manager, she oversees science at scale, running trials, managing technology, and working hands-on with livestock to measure feed efficiency and greenhouse gas emissions. The data feeds directly into the wider New Zealand beef and dairy genetics industry. Diane built her path to this role through strong relationships within Pāmu, stepping up from Facility Coordinator to run the entire daily operation. She weaves te ao Māori into her daily management style, viewing her work at the facility as kaitiakitanga in action, caring for the land, the livestock, and the resources for future generations. "Growing up connected to whenua and whakapapa has given me a grounded lens, one that sees beyond productivity and profit to the longer-term responsibility we carry as farmers and kaitiaki of the land." For Diane, excellence means high operational standards, total proficiency, and working shoulder-to-shoulder with her farm team, researchers, and geneticists.     Pāmu Landcorp Farming Limited CEO Mark Leslie joined Mei Heron on BNZ Business Breakfast yesterday to talk about a new initiative with BNZ focused on supporting existing native forests on farms and improving biodiversity outcomes. Across New Zealand, many farms have areas of native forest that already play an important role in biodiversity and climate resilience, but also require ongoing investment in work such as pest control, planting and restoration. This initiative creates a new way to recognise the value of those existing native forests, with revenue directed back into work that helps protect and enhance them over time.     New Zealand farmers have always tried to get the best out of every part of their property, while protecting it for the generations who'll farm it next. A week ago, Pāmu and BNZ began exploring a new way to do that. New Zealand's native forests do important work in storing carbon, reducing run-off, and supporting biodiversity, but it often has no clear way to fund its own upkeep. Investment has traditionally gone into planting new forests, while existing native areas are left without the resources they need. Our partnership with BNZ changes that. Established native forest on our Mahiwi Farm in northern Hawke's Bay, soon to be QEII covenanted, now generates income: BNZ pays to bring that carbon removal into its business, and that funding goes straight back into the land, through pest control and plantings. Rather than waiting decades for new plantings to mature, this approach starts from what already exists, turning areas that previously had limited return, into something that supports both the environment and the farm business. The bush block, the riparian margin, the steep face that was never going to carry stock: these areas don't have to sit outside the farm system. This model shows they can be brought into it deliberately, contributing to both environmental outcomes and the long-term performance of the business. Our hope is that this is just the start, and that similar models will emerge to give other landowners and catchment groups with native forest on their land, large or small, the same opportunity. We're proud at Pāmu to be backing this kind of innovation, alongside our long-standing QEII covenant work, which now protects more than 10,000 hectares across our farms. It's about every hectare working, in the fullest sense, for the land and for the generations who'll inherit it. Read the full announcement below.

    Pāmu and Bank of New Zealand have partnered to trial a new process. It rewards farmers who have existing protected native areas, by offering native carbon removals to corporate entities who currently purchase overseas credits instead. 🌳 This new approach does not generate carbon credits. Instead, it uses a carbon lease arrangement to generate revenue from established native blocks and is contingent on reinvestment in activities that are aimed to increase the carbon sink over time. Activities may include pest control, removal of wilding pines, additional planting appropriate to the NZ context. A key benefit of this approach is the upfront investment to activate change. Currently, native forests planted before 1990 do not qualify for the Emissions Trading Scheme, which means until now the early adopters of land retirement and QEII covenants have been excluded. This approach values the contribution of established native bush today and provides a practical way to enable further enhancement and support climate resilience on farm. 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐬 - Businesses looking to account for carbon removals place a lease over the native forest land - The lease gives the landowner revenue from a pre-existing asset - The majority of the funding will go directly into growing the native carbon sink and enhancing biodiversity Pāmu and BNZ are starting with a 600-hectare native block in northern Hawke's Bay, which will soon be a QEII National Trust covenant.  CarbonCrop will provide the platform to measure, monitor, allocate, trace, and report GHG data, which will subsequently be audited by an independent external party. The project is designed to adhere to Greenhouse Gas Protocol Corporate and Land Sector and Removals Standards, ISO 14064-1 requirements, and Toitū Envirocare Net Carbon Zero programme requirements.  Read the full announcement here: https://lnkd.in/eC9nnQFy
